author: Blyth, 1849

art.subject: Blyth's Reed Warbler (Acrocephalus dumetorum), adult (sexes alike) in autumn: upperparts plain cold olive-brown to greyish-brown with no rufous on the rump; a short whitish supercilium, most obvious in front of the eye and fading just behind it; dark lores; throat white; underparts off-white with a faint buffish-grey wash on the breast sides and flanks; wings plain, the tertials uniform with little contrast; tail plain brown; bill dark with a pale pinkish lower mandible; dark eye; greyish-brown legs.
art.pose: perched in a leafy shrub, side view
art.scene: shrubby woodland edge on a Korean offshore island during autumn migration in September, soft light; no people, buildings or text
art.build: A small, plain reed warbler, about sparrow length but slimmer, much smaller than an Oriental Reed Warbler; round-headed with a fairly steep forehead. Bill fairly long and thin, slightly shorter than the head. Legs medium, greyish. Wings short and rounded: the primary projection is short, clearly shorter than the tertials. Tail medium, rounded, plain, without white. Often found in bushes and woodland edges rather than reeds.
avoid: Do not paint a long supercilium running well behind the eye or a dark line above it (Black-browed Reed or Paddyfield Warbler).
Do not paint a rufous rump or warm tawny upperparts; the upperparts are cold olive-brown.
Do not paint streaks on the back or breast.
Do not make it large and heavy-billed like Oriental Reed Warbler.
